title: Standing out from the noise: make your pitch work even when attention is scarce
summary: Jason Cohen argues that a pitch must survive real-world distraction, not just ideal full-attention conditions. Like Snoop Dogg testing tracks on a crackly cassette player, test your messaging in noisy conditions, check that fragments still intrigue, and repeat your message so some of it breaks through.

principles.text: Test your pitch under bad conditions: if it works through noise and distraction, it works anywhere.
principles.quote: If it sounds good on crap, it will sound good anywhere.

principles.text: Your real competition is for attention, not just rival products, features or benefits.
principles.quote: These aren't even "competitors" in the "products, features, services, benefits" sense. It's competition for *attention*.

principles.text: Record your spoken pitch in a noisy place and check it still makes sense with only part of it audible.
principles.quote: Record your pitch in a noisy environment (a bar, a playground). Play it back; does it still make sense when you can only make out sixty percent of the syllables?

principles.text: Printed material should be eye-catching in fragments, so partial glimpses still spark interest.
principles.quote: Your entire message doesn't need to shine through, but is it eye-catching enough for someone to notice the fragments, to become interested?

principles.text: Repeat your message across channels, since distractions will block most single exposures.
principles.quote: Repeating often enough (using newsletters, blog, Twitter, Facebook) can push *some* of your communications through the chaos.

principles.text: Don't rely on a captive audience; a pitch that only works with full attention will fail in practice.
principles.quote: It's not enough to be compelling when you have 60 uninterrupted, full-attention seconds.
